implementation_notes: The standard library's ast module is this pattern in Python: ast.AST is the base of all node classes, each concrete class declares _fields ('the names of all child nodes'), and the generic machinery - ast.iter_child_nodes, ast.walk, ast.NodeVisitor, ast.dump - traverses any node without knowing node-specific attributes. A hand-written DSL can subclass ast.AST, set _fields and call the base constructor, then reuse that machinery unchanged; the alternative is plain classes or dataclasses with an explicit children() protocol, which is what most third-party parsers do when they want their own conventions. Prefer the stdlib form when generic tooling matters, hand-rolled dataclasses when strict typed attributes matter more.
pitfalls: iter_child_nodes only sees fields that are both listed in _fields and present as attributes: a child set under another name or left unassigned is invisible to every generic pass.
Compiling a tree that was not produced by the parser requires line/column attributes - use ast.fix_missing_locations before compile().
Recursive walkers (including the ast module's own) hit the interpreter recursion limit on deep trees; large inputs need an explicit stack.
